extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and students in media studies, criminology, sociology, and communications studying racial/ethnic representations in news
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing TV crime news race portrayals
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analysis and multivariate modeling of television news stories to measure how race/ethnicity of perpetrators and victims are represented, and how story situational features and DMA (Designated Market Area) context predict those representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and exclusion of stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Include only news stories that make explicit mention of current, specific violent crimes; exclude stories about violent crime as a general phenomenon (no specific crime), policy or program stories, civil cases (unless they involve a violent crime), terrorism, sports violence during an event, government-sponsored violence, historical violent crimes (e.g., well-known historic assassinations), and uncontrolled animal attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures the sample focuses on discrete, reportable violent incidents. Identification of qualifying stories was double-coded on randomly-selected subsamples at multiple coding stages to assess reliability (Cohen's kappas reported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling design (constructed month and DMA stratification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratified random sample of television news stories broadcast in 2002 and 2003 using a constructed month (four weeks) stratified by quarter and day of week; on each selected date, one DMA per market-size stratum was randomly selected and the evening news broadcast from one local TV station was sampled; national network broadcasts (ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC) were sampled separately each day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DMA strata divided into six strata by market size so population percent served is roughly equal across strata; balances network affiliations and includes both local and national broadcasts. Use of constructed month controls for seasonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis and temporal/generalizability constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses are limited to stories broadcast in 2002–2003; inferences are therefore about coverage during those years though authors argue patterns likely stable over the short intervening years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the sample years when generalizing findings; consider whether temporal change may affect applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding procedures and coder training
rubrics_metrics.description: Content coding performed by two trained graduate student coders under the lead researcher who met regularly to refine the coding scheme and discuss discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular meetings to refine coding and discuss discrepancies are required. Double-coding of random subsamples at outset and at 25%, 50%, and 75% of programs was used to monitor reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-coder reliability standards and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Report Cohen's kappa for identification and key variables (e.g., identifying qualifying stories, perpetrator ethnicity, victim ethnicity, number of victims, victim gender, type of violent crime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors reported kappas ranging e.g., .76–.9 for story ID; .86 for perpetrator ethnicity; .83–.95 for victim ethnicity; .73–.80 for number of victims; .89–.94 for victim gender; .72–.84 for type of violent crime. Interpret kappas using standards (e.g., Landis & Koch) and state that these levels indicate very good reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome variable categories for race/ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Code race/ethnicity of perpetrators and victims using five nominal categories: White (reference), Black, Hispanic, Other, Not indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When race/ethnicity cannot be determined by specified indicators (see determination methods), code as 'Not indicated'. Report category percentages and use White as base/reference in multinomial models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for determining perpetrator/victim race-ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine race/ethnicity from the news content via one or more indicators: person shown on tape, mug shot, artist's sketch, photo, explicit statement of race/ethnicity (or inference from a stated surname), family member shown, or corroboration from a different news report on the same incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document which indicator(s) were used and use consistent rules for coding; if multiple indicators conflict, follow documented hierarchy (not explicitly stated beyond prevalence rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding rule for multiple perpetrators
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple perpetrators are present, assign the race-ethnicity of the most prevalent group; if equal numbers from different racial/ethnic groups, code the minority group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a deterministic tie-breaker to preserve minority representation rather than defaulting to majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding rule for multiple victims and victim gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple Victims is a dummy indicator (more than one victim vs single); Female Victim is a dummy (victim female vs male). If multiple victims, assign the more common gender; if there are equal numbers, code as female.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tie-breaker prioritizes female victim identification in ties. Also a separate White Female Victim dummy is used to test unique effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of violent index crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify incidents as violent index crimes (dummy) when they involve homicide, robbery, murder-suicide, assault, or sexual assault; non-index crimes include events such as kidnapping, car jacking, breaking and entering with persons in home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use FBI violent index definitions as guidance; explicitly state included offenses and treat index/non-index as a key situational predictor.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMA-context variables (operationalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure DMA-level context by aggregating county-level census counts to DMA: percent non-Hispanic White, percent non-Hispanic Black, percent Hispanic (any race), percent Other (non-Hispanic Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, other or multiple races), and violent index crime rate per 100,000 residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 2000 Census for demographic variables and FBI Uniform Crime Reports (2002–2003) for crime rates; document aggregation and county-to-DMA mapping (Broadcasting and Cable Yearbook).

rubrics_metrics.name: DMA assignment rules and geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Define DMAs using the Broadcasting and Cable Yearbook (2002–2003) county composition; whole counties are assigned to only one DMA; DMAs vary widely in population and together cover the continental U.S., Hawaii and parts of Alaska.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how counties map to DMAs and how DMA population measures are constructed; note that national networks use nation-level characteristics as their 'DMA'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control variables: population size and region
rubrics_metrics.description: Control for DMA population size (number of persons from 2000 census) and region via dummy variables for Northeast, Midwest, South, West with the United States (national) as the reference category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these controls because population and region relate to crime prevalence and news coverage patterns; report reference categories explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling: multinomial logistic regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multinomial logistic regression to analyze five-category unordered outcomes (race/ethnicity of perpetrator and victim), reporting odds ratios and robust standard errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base outcome set to White; present likelihood ratio index to assess model improvement and report percent in each outcome category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for clustering and robust standard errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnose clustering effects by constructing five dichotomous contrasts (each outcome category vs all others) and estimate random effects binomial logistic regressions clustered by date and by DMA; use likelihood-ratio tests to decide which clustering (date or DMA) is significant and calculate robust standard errors accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors found clustering by date was important (LR tests significant) but not clustering by DMA, so they used robust SEs correcting for clustering by date in the reported multinomial models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic and sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct supplementary analyses to test robustness: e.g., homicide-only models, analyses limited to local news broadcasts, and checks adding situational measures such as story length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whether supplemental analyses produce comparable results or identify systematic differences; omit non-significant supplemental measures from main reports (e.g., story length was tested but not reported because it was not significant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of sexual assault cases for victim ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of confidentiality and small cell counts, sexual assault is used only as a predictor for the 'race/ethnicity not indicated' category; sexual assault stories increase the likelihood that a victim's race/ethnicity is not identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cell counts are too small for reliable estimation for other outcome categories, restrict use of predictors to categories where estimation is reliable and document rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting conventions and significance thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Report odds ratios with standard errors (in parentheses), provide significance markers (authors used * for p<.05 one-tailed, ** for p<.01 one-tailed, *** for p<.001 one-tailed, and † for p<.05 two-tailed), and include model fit statistics (log likelihood, Likelihood Ratio Index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the hypothesis-testing conventions (one-tailed vs two-tailed) used and the base/reference categories for interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical framing as evaluative lenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple theoretical perspectives to generate hypotheses about representation patterns: power structure (media reflect views of powerful/White owners), market share (media cater to largest audience), normal crimes (newsworthiness tied to departures from 'normal' high-status profiles), racial threat (greater minority presence/violence increases portrayals as perpetrators), and racial privileging (privileged treatment of Whites in reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly derive competing expectations from each perspective about whether groups will be over- or under-represented as perpetrators or victims and about which situational/contextual factors should matter; use empirical results to adjudicate among perspectives.
